notes.meaning: Sarai still had no children, even though God had promised Abram a large family. She owned an Egyptian servant named Hagar, whom she likely received while living in Egypt.

Sarai told Abram to have a child with Hagar so they could build a family through her. Abram agreed to her plan instead of asking the Lord for guidance. Taking matters into our own hands often brings trouble instead of peace.

differ.view: Many Reformed teachers see Abram listening to Sarai as a parallel to Adam listening to Eve, viewing this as a spiritual fall in Abram's life.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Ancient legal texts like the Nuzi tablets show that a barren wife in that culture had a recognized right to give a servant to her husband to bear children.

notes.meaning: Abram had lived in Canaan for ten years before Sarai gave Hagar to him as a second wife. Ten years was a long time to wait, and their patience had worn thin.
Abram slept with Hagar and she became pregnant. As soon as Hagar knew she was expecting a baby, she began to look down on Sarai and treat her with disrespect.
Sarai became angry and blamed Abram for the disrespect she was receiving from her servant. She even asked the Lord to judge between the two of them, speaking out of wounded pride.
Abram put Hagar back under Sarai's authority rather than managing the conflict himself. Sarai treated Hagar so harshly that the pregnant servant ran away into the desert.
The Angel of the Lord found Hagar resting by a spring of water in the wilderness. She was on the road to Shur, heading back toward her original homeland of Egypt.

The Angel addressed her as Sarai's servant to remind her of her place and duties. He asked where she came from and where she was going, and Hagar honestly admitted she was running away from her mistress.
The Angel told Hagar to go back to Sarai and submit to her authority. God called her to humble herself and return to her post, even though her mistress had been unkind.

The Angel promised to give Hagar so many descendants that no one would be able to count them. Because the speaker promised to do what only God can do, Christian interpreters traditionally see this Angel as the Lord Himself.
The Angel told Hagar she would give birth to a son and must name him Ishmael, which means 'God hears.' God chose this name because He had heard her cry in her misery.
The Angel said Ishmael would be like a wild donkey, loving freedom and refusing to be tamed. He would live in conflict with those around him and yet maintain his own ground near his relatives.
Hagar gave the Lord the name 'the God who sees me.' She was astonished that she had encountered God in the desert and still lived to tell about it.
The well was named Beer-lahai-roi, which means 'the well of the Living One who sees me.' It served as a lasting reminder of how God cared for an afflicted servant girl in the desert.
Hagar returned home and gave birth to a baby boy. Abram believed her account of God's message and named the child Ishmael, exactly as the Angel had directed.
Abram was eighty-six years old when Ishmael was born. It would be another fourteen years before Isaac, the child God had promised through Sarai, was born.
